planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks earlier, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Oxford Blue blooms best without rich soil or heavy feeding.

directions: Oxford Blue is the deep violet-blue member of the classic painted sage bract series, its papery, veined terminal bracts holding rich indigo-purple color for weeks in the garden and even longer once cut and air-dried. Unlike most flowering annuals, the true flowers are tiny and nearly hidden, so the bracts carry the entire ornamental display from midsummer into fall. Keep the soil on the lean side, since overly rich ground produces lush foliage at the expense of bract color. Cut stems for drying just as the bracts reach full color, before any fading or browning sets in.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks earlier, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Pink Sunday carries the same papery, veined bracts typical of painted sage, but in a soft rose-pink shade that reads gentler in the garden than the bolder purple and blue tones of its series-mates. The true flowers are tiny and tucked inside the colorful bracts, which hold their color on the plant for weeks and dry beautifully for everlasting arrangements. Grow it in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, since rich or overly fertile ground encourages floppy growth and fewer, less vivid bracts. Shear spent stems to tidy the planting, or leave some in place to self-sow for a repeat display the following year.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks earlier, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: White Swan produces clean, pure-white bracts that brighten the border and provide a neutral, versatile color for mixed cut-flower and dried-flower arrangements alongside its blue- and pink-bracted series-mates. Like other painted sage selections, the real flowers are tiny and visually unimportant, while the showy bracts persist for weeks on the plant and keep their color well after cutting and air-drying. Grow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, since excess fertility produces more leaf and less bract color. Cut for drying as bracts reach full size, and allow some stems to set seed if self-sowing for next year is wanted.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or set out container plants after frost danger passes, in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun.

directions: White Porcelain is a clean white-flowered selection of mealy cup sage, carrying the same white-felted, mealy-textured stems and calyces as the species but replacing its violet-blue spikes with pure white blooms held on upright, well-branched stems from late spring through hard frost. It pairs easily with blue-flowered Victoria Blue or other salvias for a crisp two-tone bedding display, or stands alone as a cooling accent among warmer summer colors. Like the species it is highly heat- and drought-tolerant once established, needing little beyond occasional deep watering during extended dry spells. Shear spent flower spikes by about half in midsummer to tidy the planting and encourage a fuller fall flush.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously.

directions: Masquerade forms a compact mound of narrow, dark green leaves marked with an irregular, streaky creamy-white center, a less stable and more variable variegation pattern than the broad, defined margins of many modern hostas. It has been used more as a breeding parent than as a common garden plant in its own right, having passed its streaked center and compact habit into later hybrids such as 'Dixie Chick.' Pale lavender flowers rise on short scapes above the foliage in summer, though the foliage remains the main attraction. Because streaked variegation can be unstable, watch for shoots that revert toward solid green and divide those out to keep the clump true to type.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving some morning sun to deepen the foliage color.

directions: Brownies carries the heat and humidity tolerance of its Heuchera villosa parentage into rounded, ruffled leaves in warm milk-chocolate brown tones that hold their color better through Southern summers than many purple-leaved heuchera hybrids. Airy sprays of small white flowers rise on wiry stems above the foliage in late summer, later than most heuchera cultivars bloom, extending the season of interest. It tolerates considerably more heat, humidity, and drought than hybrids bred from northern species, making it a sturdier long-term choice for Gulf South and southeastern gardens. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, resetting the crown at its original depth as it naturally rises above the soil over time.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in spring, spacing generously for good air circulation.

directions: Omega bears dense, cylindrical clusters of white flowers marked with a small pink eye at the center of each petal, a classic pairing in the Dutch-bred meadow phlox line that also produced the pink-and-white striped sport 'Natascha.' Like other meadow phlox selections it blooms a couple of weeks earlier than tall garden phlox and shows notably better resistance to powdery mildew, an important advantage in hot, humid summers. Give it fertile, evenly moist soil and generous spacing between clumps to keep air moving through the foliage and further reduce disease pressure. Deadhead spent flower heads to tidy the planting and prevent volunteer seedlings that may not match the parent's color.

planting.note: Direct sow after cold-moist stratification, or plant container-grown divisions, in well-drained, average soil in full sun in spring.

directions: Ruby Giant is an older, large-flowered purple coneflower selection valued for its oversized blooms and sturdy, well-branched stems, qualities that later made it a popular parent plant in modern coneflower breeding programs. Its broad, slightly reflexed rose-purple ray petals surround a prominent orange-brown cone, opening from midsummer into fall on upright stems that rarely need staking. Like the species it is an easy, drought-tolerant prairie perennial once established, drawing bees and butterflies throughout its long bloom season. Deadhead to prolong flowering, or leave the spiny seed heads standing into winter to feed goldfinches.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
